SCOPE: Cost-Efficient Model Selection for Compound AI Systems under Quality Constraints

Conference: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2; August 09–13, 2026; Jeju Island, Republic of KoreaProceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2 (KDD ’26), August 09–13, 2026, Jeju Island, Republic of KoreaDOI: 10.1145/3770855.3818067ISBN: 979-8-4007-2259-2/2026/08
Yiqian Huang Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore email: yiqian@comp.nus.edu.sg , Shiqi Zhang Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore Affiliation: PyroWis AI, Singapore email: shiqi@pyrowis.ai , Tianyuan Jin Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), China email: tianyuan1044@gmail.com and Xiaokui Xiao Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore email: xkxiao@nus.edu.sg

Abstract.

A compound AI system consists of multiple LLM modules, together handling complex and multi-step tasks that exceed the capabilities of a single model. Existing systems often use a single expensive LLM across all modules to improve the result quality of the whole system. However, this configuration incurs prohibitive costs, particularly for data management and analytics tasks at scale, such as data manipulation. To this end, we formalize the problem of constrained LLM selection for compound AI systems, leveraging the diverse pricing and capabilities of different LLMs to achieve competitive quality at lower cost. Given a query dataset and a user-specified quality threshold, we aim to select an LLM for each module to minimize the system’s average cost while ensuring that overall quality meets the required threshold. To solve this problem, we propose SCOPE, a cost-efficient optimization algorithm. Unlike existing approaches that rely on expensive dataset-level evaluations, SCOPE exploits per-query results to rapidly estimate the system’s cost and quality, and constructs confidence bounds to guide the search for promising LLM combinations. Furthermore, SCOPE provides theoretical guarantees for meeting the quality threshold and achieving near-optimal average cost. We evaluate SCOPE against 7 baselines on three data processing tasks, demonstrating that it outperforms all baselines. Under the same search budget and quality constraint, it finds solutions with up to 20×20\times lower cost than the best competitor during the search and achieves up to 6×6\times lower final cost in the returned solution.

1. Introduction

A compound AI system is a multi-module system in which each module is implemented by a specific agent powered by a large language model (LLM). The system as a whole processes complex and multi-step tasks beyond the capability of any single model and thus finds applications in many scenarios, such as question answering (Huang et al., 2025b), software development (Hong et al., 2024), and data processing (Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023; Qian et al., 2024). To ensure high result quality, existing compound AI systems typically use a state-of-the-art LLM for every module and emphasize frontier system design. However, more advanced LLMs typically incur higher inference costs. This monetary overhead becomes prohibitive for tasks that require digesting large volumes of data, which is common in the data management and analytics area (Li et al., 2023). To exemplify, in data imputation, which fills missing entries in a table based on observed values, employing the flagship GPT-5.2 (OpenAI, 2025) across all modules of UniDM (Qian et al., 2024) costs around $180,000180,000 on a dataset with one million rows, each containing ten entities with rich semantic value spaces.

To mitigate this immense overhead, we formalize a new problem, constrained LLM selection for compound AI systems, which shifts the goal from quality alone to explicitly accounting for cost. Given an NN-module compound AI system, a candidate LLM set, a query dataset, and a quality threshold, this problem aims to assign a specific LLM to each module to minimize the system’s average cost over the dataset while ensuring that the average quality meets the threshold. This formulation exploits the cost–quality Pareto frontier observed in modern LLMs (Zhang et al., 2025), where models exhibit diverse pricing and complementary capabilities, creating a rich search space for optimization. By aligning model capabilities with the varying complexity of module-specific tasks, constrained LLM selection for compound AI systems admits solutions that achieve high quality at significantly lower cost.

Solving this problem remains challenging, since one must carefully balance cost and quality, using only limited observations of the system’s performance on the given dataset. A natural approach is to treat the system as a black box and apply generic constrained optimization methods, such as Bayesian optimization (Wang et al., 2025; Watanabe and Hutter, 2023) and bandit algorithms (Xu et al., 2023; Sui et al., 2015). Specifically, these solutions search over possible LLM assignments without knowing the system’s internal structure, yet they fail to guarantee convergence to a near-optimal assignment that satisfies the quality constraint at minimum cost. Moreover, they require a prohibitive number of trials, each of which executes the system on the entire dataset, often incurring search costs that even exceed the potential savings. Recently, compound-AI-specific methods (Russo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a) attempt to accelerate the search by making strong structural assumptions. For instance, Abacus (Russo et al., 2025) assumes independence between modules to estimate total cost and quality, while LLMSelector (Chen et al., 2025a) relies on monotonicity, assuming that upgrading a module’s model always improves global quality. Unfortunately, these assumptions rarely hold in practice. Relying on ad-hoc heuristics without theoretical guarantees, these methods often fail to strictly satisfy the quality threshold.

To bridge this gap, we propose SCOPE, a cost-efficient optimization algorithm with rigorous theoretical guarantees. In contrast to existing methods that rely on coarse-grained dataset-level evaluations, SCOPE uses a query-level search strategy. Specifically, it treats individual query evaluations as atomic observations to iteratively tighten statistically valid confidence bounds on both cost and quality. The query-level granularity allows the algorithm to quickly prune suboptimal LLM assignments without full-dataset evaluations, while the confidence bounds guide the search toward near-optimal solutions in a principled way. To the best of our knowledge, SCOPE is the first to provide theoretical guarantees for this noisy constrained optimization problem, ensuring that the returned solution simultaneously (i) satisfies the quality threshold with high probability and (ii) has a cost that converges to the optimum as the search budget increases. In experiments, we extensively evaluate SCOPE against seven competitors across three distinct data processing tasks involving compound AI systems. Our evaluation spans a massive search space of tens of candidate models and millions of potential LLM assignments. Notably, SCOPE strictly satisfies the quality constraint while reducing average costs by over 20×\times compared to the best competing baseline. Even at the maximum budget, it achieves a 6×\times cost reduction. Furthermore, on test-time datasets, SCOPE demonstrates robust generalization, attaining an average cost of 2–5% of a high-quality reference configuration while maintaining competitive average quality.

To summarize, we make the following contributions in this work:

  • •

    We formalize constrained LLM selection for compound AI systems as a constrained optimization problem (Section 2).

  • •

    We propose SCOPE, a cost-efficient optimization algorithm that reduces the search cost (Section 3).

  • •

    We provide theoretical guarantees on both the cost and the quality of the solution returned by SCOPE (Section 4).

  • •

    We conduct experiments showing that SCOPE outperforms existing methods (Section 6).

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Problem Formulation

Compound AI system. Consider a query dataset 𝒬\mathcal{Q} (where |𝒬|=Q|\mathcal{Q}|=Q), a set of candidate LLMs ℳ\mathcal{M} (where |ℳ|=M|\mathcal{M}|=M), and a compound AI system consisting of NN modules, each integrated with an LLM. A configuration is defined as a vector 𝜽=[θ1,…,θN]\bm{\theta}=[\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}], where each θi∈ℳ\theta_{i}\in\mathcal{M} denotes the LLM selected for the ii-th module. The configuration space is denoted by Θ=ℳN\Theta=\mathcal{M}^{N}, representing the set of all possible configurations. For a configuration 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta and a query q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}, system execution is measured by two metrics:

  • •

    ℓs​(𝜽,q)∈[0,1]\ell_{s}(\bm{\theta},q)\in[0,1], the expected quality (e.g., accuracy) of the system’s output on query qq under configuration 𝜽\bm{\theta};

  • •

    ℓc​(𝜽,q)∈[Cmin,Cmax]\ell_{c}(\bm{\theta},q)\in[C_{\min},C_{\max}], the corresponding expected monetary cost, bounded by known limits CminC_{\min} and CmaxC_{\max}.

We focus on the average quality and average cost over the dataset 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, which are defined, respectively, as

c⁡(𝜽)=1Q​∑q∈𝒬ℓc​(𝜽,q),s⁡(𝜽)=1Q​∑q∈𝒬ℓs​(𝜽,q).c(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\ell_{c}(\bm{\theta},q),\quad s(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\ell_{s}(\bm{\theta},q).

In practice, users typically begin with a reference configuration 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} (e.g., employing a powerful LLM for all modules), which yields high quality s⁡(𝜽0)s(\bm{\theta}_{0}) but incurs a high cost. Given ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) specifying the maximum allowable quality degradation, we define the quality threshold as s0=(1−ϵ)⋅s⁡(𝜽0)s_{0}=(1-\epsilon)\cdot s(\bm{\theta}_{0}). Let g⁡(𝜽)=s0−s⁡(𝜽)g(\bm{\theta})=s_{0}-s(\bm{\theta}) and ℓg​(𝜽,q)=s0−ℓs​(𝜽,q)\ell_{g}(\bm{\theta},q)=s_{0}-\ell_{s}(\bm{\theta},q) for each q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}. We define constrained LLM selection for compound AI systems as follows.

Problem 1 (Constrained LLM Selection for Compound AI Systems).

Given an NN-module compound AI system, a dataset 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, a configuration space Θ=ℳN\Theta=\mathcal{M}^{N}, and a reference configuration 𝜽0∈Θ\bm{\theta}_{0}\in\Theta with known quality s⁡(𝜽0)s(\bm{\theta}_{0}), the objective is to find a configuration that minimizes the average cost while satisfying the quality constraint:

(1) 𝜽⋆∈argmin𝜽∈Θ:g⁡(𝜽)≤0c(𝜽).\displaystyle\bm{\theta}^{\star}\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta:~g(\bm{\theta})\leq 0}c(\bm{\theta}).

A configuration 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta is called feasible if it satisfies g⁡(𝜽)≤0g(\bm{\theta})\leq 0. By definition, 𝜽⋆\bm{\theta}^{\star} exists since at least one configuration 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} is feasible.

Notations. Throughout this paper, we denote [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\} and ℕ={0,1,…}\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\dots\}. A boldface lowercase letter 𝒙\bm{x} represents a vector, and a boldface uppercase letter 𝑿\bm{X} represents a matrix, where (𝑿)a,b(\bm{X})_{a,b} denotes the value in its aa-th row and bb-th column. An algorithm for Problem 1 runs over discrete time steps t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}. At each time tt, it selects a pair (𝜽t,qt)∈Θ×𝒬(\bm{\theta}_{t},q_{t})\in\Theta\times\mathcal{Q} to evaluate (hereafter, to observe) and receives a pair of noisy observations of ℓc​(𝜽t,qt)\ell_{c}(\bm{\theta}_{t},q_{t}) and ℓg​(𝜽t,qt)\ell_{g}(\bm{\theta}_{t},q_{t}), denoted by (yc,t,yg,t)(y_{c,t},y_{g,t}). 2.2. Existing Solutions

Problem 1 is challenging because both cc and gg are expensive black-box functions that do not admit closed-form expressions. A natural baseline is to cast it as a generic constrained optimization problem, where one has access only to noisy observations (i.e., values with random noise) of c⁡(𝜽)c(\bm{\theta}) and g⁡(𝜽)g(\bm{\theta}). Under this framing, one could apply sequential search methods for constrained optimization, such as constrained Bayesian optimization, among others (Xu et al., 2023; Sui et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2025; Watanabe and Hutter, 2023; Zhou and Ji, 2022).

Generic optimization approaches. Generic optimization methods, such as Bayesian optimization (BO) (Wang et al., 2025; Watanabe and Hutter, 2023) and bandit algorithms (Xu et al., 2023; Sui et al., 2015; Zhou and Ji, 2022), have been used to tune compound AI systems for cost or quality (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024; Khattab et al., 2024; He et al., 2025), and can be rigorously extended to handle the quality constraint. In the unconstrained setting, these methods come with theoretical guarantees in terms of regret, which quantify how quickly the returned configuration approaches the optimal configuration. Such guarantees typically rely on standard assumptions: informally, similar configurations yield similar function values, so that past evaluations can generalize to unobserved configurations.

Compound-AI-specific approaches. Other recent methods aim to improve empirical search efficiency by making extra assumptions about the compound AI system, rather than treating it as a pure black box. For example, Abacus (Russo et al., 2025), the optimizer used by Palimpzest (Liu et al., 2025), estimates c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot) and s⁡(⋅)s(\cdot) by assuming independence across modules and employing additive or multiplicative estimators. LLMSelector (Chen et al., 2025a) assumes that quality is monotonically non-decreasing when upgrading LLMs according to a fixed ranking, and accordingly proposes a round-robin procedure that updates one module at a time. LLAMBO (Liu et al., 2024) treats the LLM itself as an estimation model, using its internal knowledge and the observation history to predict the cost and quality of unseen configurations.

Limitations. Existing approaches have two main limitations in the noisy constrained setting (Xu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025). First, it is hard for them to guarantee correctness and effectiveness at the same time. Here, correctness means the returned solution 𝜽out\bm{\theta}_{\rm out} is feasible, i.e., g⁡(𝜽out)≤0g(\bm{\theta}_{\rm out})\leq 0, and effectiveness means its cost is close to the best feasible value, i.e., c⁡(𝜽out)≈c⁡(𝜽⋆)c(\bm{\theta}_{\rm out})\approx c(\bm{\theta}^{\star}). For instance, methods such as CONFIG (Xu et al., 2023) prioritize effectiveness but risk violating correctness, while SafeOpt (Sui et al., 2015) ensures correctness but often converges to suboptimal solutions. While recent work on constrained expected improvement (cEI) (Wang et al., 2025), a variant of constrained BO, theoretically addresses both, it relies on a noiseless assumption (i.e., without random noise) that does not hold for stochastic LLM outputs. Second, existing approaches remain cost-inefficient as they do not fully exploit query-level signals ℓc\ell_{c} and ℓg\ell_{g}. By treating average cost and average quality as pure black-box functions, these methods must evaluate configurations on the entire dataset 𝒬\mathcal{Q} to obtain an observed signal for average cost or quality. As shown in Section 6, fully evaluating an infeasible configuration with Q=500Q=500 can cost around $12\$12, whereas analyzing just a few queries using ℓc\ell_{c} and ℓg\ell_{g} could reveal infeasibility immediately. Yet, it remains an open problem to exploit query-level signals without compromising theoretical guarantees. These limitations motivate a principled solution that addresses Problem 1 by integrating rigorous guarantees with a cost-efficient, query-level evaluation scheme.

3. SCOPE

We propose Sequential Confidence-bound-based Optimization via Partial Evaluation (SCOPE), which solves Problem 1 with guarantees of correctness and effectiveness. When Q=1Q=1, SCOPE also applies to generic noisy constrained optimization.

3.1. Main Procedure

At the core of SCOPE are carefully designed confidence bounds for the cost c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot) and the constraint g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot). Given a failure probability δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), for time t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, configuration 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta, and function ζ∈{c,g}\zeta\in\{c,g\}, SCOPE maintains lower and upper bounds Lζ,t​(𝜽)L_{\zeta,t}(\bm{\theta}) and Uζ,t​(𝜽)U_{\zeta,t}(\bm{\theta}) such that they enclose the true function values with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta:

(2) Pr[∀ζ,t,𝜽:Lζ,t(𝜽)≤ζ(𝜽)≤Uζ,t(𝜽)]≥1−δ.\Pr\left[\forall\zeta,t,\bm{\theta}:\ L_{\zeta,t}(\bm{\theta})\leq\zeta(\bm{\theta})\leq U_{\zeta,t}(\bm{\theta})\right]\geq 1-\delta.

Building on these bounds, SCOPE proceeds in iterations. In each iteration i∈{1,2,…}i\in\{1,2,\dots\}, SCOPE selects a candidate configuration 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} that is promising under the current bounds and then evaluates 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} sequentially on queries in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} until the search budget is exhausted. Notably, the guarantees of SCOPE are ensured by two key mechanisms.

  1. (1)

    Candidate selection: In iteration ii, it selects 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} using a dynamic constraint Lg,t​(𝜽)≤−i−αL_{g,t}(\bm{\theta})\leq-i^{-\alpha}, where α∈(0,1/2)\alpha\in(0,1/2) is a fixed parameter, to filter out candidates that are likely infeasible. Among the remaining candidates, 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} is chosen greedily by minimizing the cost lower bound Lc,t​(𝜽)L_{c,t}(\bm{\theta}).

  2. (2)

    Sequential query evaluation: After selecting 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand}, SCOPE evaluates it on queries q(1),…,q(Q)∈𝒬q^{(1)},\dots,q^{(Q)}\in\mathcal{Q} in decreasing order of a score φi​(q)\varphi_{i}(q). This score is defined to quantify how much information we gain from evaluating qq and, in turn, to tighten the bounds for both cc and gg using as few observations as possible.

In addition, the cost efficiency of SCOPE hinges on two further design choices that exploit query-level signals.

  1. (3)

    Bound calibration: During initialization, SCOPE invokes a subroutine, Calibrate, which calibrates accurate confidence bounds within a small initial budget.

  2. (4)

    Pruning mechanism: SCOPE incorporates a pruning mechanism enabled by the sequential, query-level evaluation. As the bounds are updated, it stops evaluating 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} early once 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} appears infeasible (i.e., Lg,t​(𝜽cand)>0L_{g,t}(\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand})>0) or cannot improve on the current best solution in terms of cost.

Algorithm 1 gives the pseudocode of SCOPE; we defer the description of Calibrate to Section 3.2 and defer the definition of Lζ,tL_{\zeta,t}, Uζ,tU_{\zeta,t}, and φi\varphi_{i} to Section 3.3. It takes four additional inputs: a search budget Λ>0\Lambda>0 which limits the cumulative monetary cost of observing yc,ty_{c,t} over time, a failure probability δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) used in the confidence bounds, a trade-off parameter α∈(0,1/2)\alpha\in(0,1/2), and a base model θbase∈ℳ\theta_{\rm base}\in\mathcal{M}, which represents a user-chosen cost-efficient LLM used by the Calibrate subroutine. In Line 1, the algorithm first invokes Calibrate with parameter θbase\theta_{\rm base}, which performs t0t_{0} initial observations, and sets t←t0t\leftarrow t_{0}. In Lines 1–1, the algorithm initializes the confidence bounds Lζ,tL_{\zeta,t} and Uζ,tU_{\zeta,t}, the current best configuration 𝜽out←𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{out}}\leftarrow\bm{\theta}_{0}, and the current best upper bound UoutU_{\rm out}. After initialization, at each outer loop ii (Line 1), SCOPE selects a configuration 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{cand}} according to the selection criterion in Line 1. Subsequently, the queries in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are ordered as q(1),…,q(Q)q^{(1)},\dots,q^{(Q)} in decreasing order of the query-wise surrogate uncertainty φi​(q(j))\varphi_{i}(q^{(j)}) (Line 1), and are sequentially evaluated with 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} in the inner jj-loop (Line 1). At each inner iteration jj, the algorithm increments the time tt by one and observes (𝜽cand,q(j))(\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand},q^{(j)}) to obtain yc,ty_{c,t} and yg,ty_{g,t} (Line 1), which in turn refines the confidence bounds at time tt. Finally, SCOPE returns (𝜽out,τ)(\bm{\theta}_{\rm out},\tau) where τ=t\tau=t represents the stopping time after which it makes no further observations.

3.2. Bound Calibration

To identify the rough scale of confidence bounds for c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot) and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot), SCOPE invokes a heuristically designed Calibrate subroutine. Calibrate proceeds in a hybrid manner: it first collects observations from a large, diverse pool of configurations using a single query, and then iteratively doubles the size of the query set while halving the configuration pool. As a result, higher-quality configurations receive additional evaluation, until a single remaining configuration in the pool is evaluated on the entire query set.

This design is motivated by three empirical observations. First, cost differences are mainly driven by the selected LLMs rather than by which query is executed, since model prices often differ by orders of magnitude. As a result, evaluating many diverse configurations on only a few queries provides early estimates of the cost scale across configurations. Second, evaluating a high-potential configuration on only a few queries is often insufficient, because the query-wise quality ℓs​(𝜽,q)\ell_{s}(\bm{\theta},q) can vary significantly across queries q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}. Given a limited search budget Λ\Lambda, we increase the number of sampled queries only for configurations that appear high-quality, to obtain a reliable estimate of their average quality. Finally, it is often beneficial to choose a lightweight model θbase\theta_{\rm base} and focus on configurations related to this model, thereby saving search cost by avoiding evaluations of configurations that include many expensive models.

The detailed pseudocode is shown in Algorithm 2, which takes as input the base model θbase∈ℳ\theta_{\rm base}\in\mathcal{M}. The subroutine first constructs an initial pool Θinit⊆Θ\Theta_{\text{init}}\subseteq\Theta as

(3) Θinit={[θ1,…,θN]∈Θ:∑i=1N𝟏{θi≠θbase}≤1},\textstyle\Theta_{\rm init}=\big\{[\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}]\in\Theta:\ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\bm{1}\{\theta_{i}\neq\theta_{\text{base}}\}\leq 1\big\},

and randomly shuffles 𝒬\mathcal{Q} as {q(1),…,q(Q)}\{q^{(1)},\dots,q^{(Q)}\}. Then, it runs for ⌈log2⁡(Q+1)⌉\lceil\log_{2}(Q+1)\rceil rounds. In round jj, it evaluates each remaining configuration in Θinit\Theta_{\text{init}} on additional queries in 𝒬j∖𝒬j−1\mathcal{Q}_{j}\setminus\mathcal{Q}_{j-1}, where 𝒬j={q(1),…,q(min⁡{2j−1,Q})}\mathcal{Q}_{j}=\{q^{(1)},\dots,q^{(\min\{2^{j-1},Q\})}\}. Afterward, it retains the top half of configurations ranked by their cumulative observed quality over 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j} and discards the rest. By the final round, the pool is reduced to a single configuration, which has been evaluated on all QQ queries.

3.3. Confidence Bounds

For each ζ∈{c,g}\zeta\in\{c,g\}, t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, and 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta, the confidence bounds in Line 1 are of the following form:

(4) Lζ,t​(𝜽)\displaystyle L_{\zeta,t}(\bm{\theta}) =μ¯ζ,t​(𝜽)−βζ,t​σ¯ζ,t​(𝜽),\displaystyle=\bar{\mu}_{\zeta,t}(\bm{\theta})-\beta_{\zeta,t}\,\bar{\sigma}_{\zeta,t}(\bm{\theta}),

4. Theoretical Analysis

4.1. Assumptions

We state the theoretical assumptions under which SCOPE’s guarantees are derived. They extend the standard frequentist setting for generic constrained optimization (Bull, 2011; Chowdhury and Gopalan, 2017; Srinivas et al., 2010) to Q≥1Q\geq 1. When Q=1Q=1, they reduce to the standard ones in (Srinivas et al., 2010). These assumptions are parameterized by Rc,Rg≥0R_{c},R_{g}\geq 0, Bc,Bg>0B_{c},B_{g}>0, and the SPD kernel kk with k⁡(𝜽,𝜽)=1k(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta})=1 for all 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta.

Assumption 1 (Sub-Gaussian noise).

The observations satisfy

(10) ∀t∈ℕ,yc,t=ℓc​(𝜽t,qt)+ηc,t,yg,t=ℓg​(𝜽t,qt)+ηg,t,\forall t\in\mathbb{N},\;\;y_{c,t}=\ell_{c}(\bm{\theta}_{t},q_{t})+\eta_{c,t},\quad y_{g,t}=\ell_{g}(\bm{\theta}_{t},q_{t})+\eta_{g,t},

where ηc,t\eta_{c,t} and ηg,t\eta_{g,t} are zero-mean random variables. For each ζ∈{c,g}\zeta\in\{c,g\}, the sequence {ηζ,t}t=1∞\{\eta_{\zeta,t}\}_{t=1}^{\infty} is conditionally RζR_{\zeta}-sub-Gaussian, i.e.,

∀t∈ℕ,∀u∈ℝ,𝔼⁡[exp⁡(u⋅ηζ,t)|ℱt−1]≤exp⁡((u2​Rζ2)/2),\forall t\in\mathbb{N},\forall u\in\mathbb{R},~\mathbb{E}[\exp{(u\cdot\eta_{\zeta,t})}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq\exp{\big({(u^{2}R_{\zeta}^{2})}/2\big)},

where ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} is the σ\sigma-algebra generated by {𝜽i,qi,yc,i,yg,i}i=1t−1\{\bm{\theta}_{i},q_{i},y_{c,i},y_{g,i}\}_{i=1}^{t-1}.

Assumption 2 (Boundedness in RKHS).

Let ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} be the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) induced by kk, with norm ∥⋅∥ℋk\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}. 11 1 Concretely, RKHS ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} is a collection of functions equipped with an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℋk\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}} such that for every 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta and f∈ℋkf\in\mathcal{H}_{k}, it holds that k⁡(𝜽,⋅)∈ℋkk(\bm{\theta},\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}_{k} and ⟨f,k⁡(𝜽,⋅)⟩ℋk=f⁡(𝜽)\langle f,k(\bm{\theta},\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}=f(\bm{\theta}). The norm is then ‖f‖ℋk=⟨f,f⟩ℋk\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}=\sqrt{\langle f,f\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}}. We assume for each q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}, ‖ℓc​(⋅,q)‖ℋk≤Bc\|\ell_{c}(\cdot,q)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}\leq B_{c} and ‖ℓg​(⋅,q)‖ℋk≤Bg\|\ell_{g}(\cdot,q)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}\leq B_{g}.

Interpretation. Regarding Assumption 1, upper bounds for RcR_{c} and RgR_{g} are often available in practice. For example, if system evaluations satisfy yc,t∈[Cmin,Cmax]y_{c,t}\in[C_{\min},C_{\max}] and yg,t∈[s0−1,s0]y_{g,t}\in[s_{0}-1,s_{0}], a sufficient choice is Rc=(Cmax−Cmin)/2R_{c}=(C_{\max}-C_{\min})/2 and Rg=1/2R_{g}=1/2. If evaluations are noiseless, it suffices to set any Rc=Rg≥0R_{c}=R_{g}\geq 0. In Assumption 2, BζB_{\zeta} bounds how similar ℓζ​(𝜽,q)\ell_{\zeta}(\bm{\theta},q) and ℓζ​(𝜽′,q)\ell_{\zeta}(\bm{\theta}^{\prime},q) are for every q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}, ζ∈{c,g}\zeta\in\{c,g\}, and 𝜽,𝜽′∈Θ\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in\Theta. In particular, one can infer the following property:

|ℓζ​(𝜽,q)−ℓζ​(𝜽′,q)|≤Bζ​2−2​k​(𝜽,𝜽′).|\ell_{\zeta}(\bm{\theta},q)-\ell_{\zeta}(\bm{\theta}^{\prime},q)|\leq B_{\zeta}\sqrt{2-2k(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})}.

Since Θ\Theta is finite in Problem 1, for any SPD kernel kk there exist Bc,Bg<∞B_{c},B_{g}<\infty such that Assumption 2 holds. In implementation, this allows us to adopt a commonly used kernel and treat BcB_{c} and BgB_{g} as hyperparameters, following prior work (Xu et al., 2023; Srinivas et al., 2010).

4.2. Guarantees

Recall that τ\tau is the stopping time after which the algorithm makes no further observations, and 𝜽out\bm{\theta}_{\rm out} is the returned configuration. We say the algorithm is δ\delta-correct if Pr[g(𝜽out)≤0]≥1−δ\Pr[g(\bm{\theta}_{\rm out})\leq 0]\geq 1-\delta, where the randomness is over the observations. We measure effectiveness by simple regret, defined as SR⁡(τ)=c⁡(𝜽out)−c⁡(𝜽⋆)\mathrm{SR}(\tau)=c(\bm{\theta}_{\rm out})-c(\bm{\theta}^{\star}), where c⁡(𝜽⋆)c(\bm{\theta}^{\star}) is the optimal cost defined in (1). The following theorem shows that the confidence bounds hold with high probability. All proofs are provided in Appendix C.

Theorem 4.1.

Fix δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). For any t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, ζ∈{c,g}\zeta\in\{c,g\}, and λ>0\lambda>0 which is used in Definition 3.1, let the confidence bounds in (4) be defined using (8) and (7). Under Assumptions 1–2, the resulting bounds satisfy the high-probability event in (2).

The next theorem shows that SCOPE is δ\delta-correct and provides an explicit upper bound on SR⁡(τ)\mathrm{SR}(\tau).

Theorem 4.2.

Fix Λ>0\Lambda>0, δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), and α∈(0,1/2)\alpha\in(0,1/2), and let t0t_{0} be the time returned by Calibrate in Line 1. Under Assumptions 1–2, SCOPE is δ\delta-correct. Moreover, for any τ\tau returned by SCOPE, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the simple regret satisfies

(11) SR⁡(τ)≤𝖠(τ−t0)−𝖡⋅(τ−t0)2​α−𝖢\mathrm{SR}(\tau)\ \leq\ \frac{\mathsf{A}}{\sqrt{(\tau-t_{0})\ -\ \mathsf{B}\cdot(\tau-t_{0})^{2\alpha}\ -\ \mathsf{C}}}

whenever g⁡(𝛉⋆)<0g(\bm{\theta}^{\star})<0 and (τ−t0)−𝖡⋅(τ−t0)2​α−𝖢>0,(\tau-t_{0})-\mathsf{B}\cdot(\tau-t_{0})^{2\alpha}-\mathsf{C}>0, where

𝖠=8βc,τQ⁡(λ+1)​γ​(τ),𝖡=16Q(λ+1)βg,τ2γ(τ),𝖢=Q⌈(−g(𝜽⋆))−1/α⌉.\begin{gathered}\mathsf{A}=8\beta_{c,\tau}\sqrt{Q(\lambda+1)\gamma(\tau)},\quad\mathsf{B}=16Q(\lambda+1)\beta_{g,\tau}^{2}\gamma(\tau),\\ \mathsf{C}=Q\lceil{(-g(\bm{\theta}^{\star})})^{-1/\alpha}\rceil.\end{gathered}

As shown in Theorem 4.2, SR⁡(τ)\mathrm{SR}(\tau) in Algorithm 1 converges at a rate of O⁡(1/τ)O(1/\sqrt{\tau}), since Θ\Theta is finite and hence γ⁡(τ)\gamma(\tau) is bounded by a constant. The parameter α\alpha trades off the (τ−t0)2​α(\tau-t_{0})^{2\alpha} term against the dependence on g⁡(𝜽⋆)g(\bm{\theta}^{\star}) via 𝖢\mathsf{C}. Since g⁡(𝜽⋆)g(\bm{\theta}^{\star}) is unknown, a convenient choice is to set α\alpha to a moderate constant, e.g., 1/31/3. The dependence on g⁡(𝜽⋆)<0g(\bm{\theta}^{\star})<0 is necessary and, as α→1/2\alpha\to 1/2, the term (−g⁡(𝜽⋆))−2(-g(\bm{\theta}^{\star}))^{-2} becomes nearly tight, in the sense that it is unavoidable in the worst case for any δ\delta-correct algorithm; see Appendix D for details. Moreover, the following corollary translates the τ\tau-based bound into an O⁡(1/Λ)O(1/\sqrt{\Lambda}) bound in expectation.

Corollary 0.

Fix α∈(0,1/2)\alpha\in(0,1/2) and suppose Assumptions 1–2 and g⁡(𝜽⋆)<0g(\bm{\theta}^{\star})<0 hold. For each search budget Λ>0\Lambda>0, let δ=Λ−2\delta=\Lambda^{-2}. Then there exists m≥2m\geq 2, independent of Λ\Lambda, such that for all Λ≥m\Lambda\geq m, 𝔼⁡[SR⁡(τ)]=O⁡((log⁡Λ)/Λ),\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SR}(\tau)]=O(\sqrt{(\log\Lambda)/\Lambda}), where the expectation is over the randomness of the observations and the stopping time τ\tau.

4.3. Computational Complexity

While simple regret captures the main search cost, we also analyze the additional computational cost to assess the practical runtime of SCOPE. In the algorithm, the time and space complexity are dominated by the selection of 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} in Line 1. As implied by (7), this step requires computing μ^𝒙q,t,𝒚ζ,q,t\hat{\mu}_{\bm{x}_{q,t},{\bm{y}}_{\zeta,q,t}} and σ^𝒙q,t,𝒚ζ,q,t\hat{\sigma}_{\bm{x}_{q,t},{\bm{y}}_{\zeta,q,t}} for all 𝜽∈Θ\bm{\theta}\in\Theta, ζ∈{c,g}\zeta\in\{c,g\}, and q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} at time tt. To compute each μ^∙\hat{\mu}_{\bullet} and σ^∙\hat{\sigma}_{\bullet}, we use standard GP updates as detailed in Chowdhury and Gopalan (2017), which costs O⁡(t2)O(t^{2}) time and O⁡(t2)O(t^{2}) space. Therefore, the time complexity of Line 1 at time tt is O⁡(|Θ|​∑q∈𝒬Jq,t2)=O⁡(Q⋅|Θ|⋅Jmax,t2).O(|\Theta|\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}J_{q,t}^{2})=O(Q\cdot|\Theta|\cdot J_{\max,t}^{2}). Summing over t∈[τ]t\in[\tau], the worst-case total time complexity of SCOPE in terms of τ\tau is

O⁡(∑t=1τQ⋅|Θ|⋅Jmax,t2)=O⁡(Q⋅|Θ|⋅τ3).O\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}Q\cdot|\Theta|\cdot J_{\max,t}^{2}\right)=O\!\left(Q\cdot|\Theta|\cdot\tau^{3}\right).

This is larger than the O⁡(|Θ|⋅τ3)O\left(|\Theta|\cdot\tau^{3}\right) running time of existing BO and bandit approaches (Wang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2023), due to the query-wise exploitation in SCOPE. In addition, computing βζ,t\beta_{\zeta,t} in (8) also involves γ⁡(J)\gamma(J) for all J≤τJ\leq\tau. Since 12​log​det(𝑰+λ−1​𝑲A)\frac{1}{2}\log\det(\bm{I}+\lambda^{-1}\bm{K}_{A}) is a non-decreasing submodular set function over A⊆ΘA\subseteq\Theta (Srinivas et al., 2010), γ⁡(J)\gamma(J) can be approximated within a constant factor using a greedy algorithm (Nemhauser et al., 1978) prior to running SCOPE. Although the obtained value may be slightly larger than the exact γ⁡(J)\gamma(J), it does not affect the correctness of Theorems 4.1-4.2, as the confidence bounds become looser but still satisfy (2). For space, standard GP computations imply that calculating the per-query GP surrogates costs O⁡(∑q∈𝒬Jq,τ2)=O⁡(Q⋅τ2)O(\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}J_{q,\tau}^{2})=O(Q\cdot\tau^{2}), plus O⁡(τ)O(\tau) to store the observation history. Note that the empirical running time can be significantly lower than the above worst-case complexity, as Jmax,tJ_{\max,t} is usually smaller than tt.

5. Additional Related Work

In this section, we review several lines of work that may seem related to ours, and explain how they differ from the setting in constrained LLM selection for compound AI systems.

Selecting a single model. A first line of work selects a single model for a single task. For instance, SpareLLM (Jo and Trummer, 2025) evaluates all candidate LLMs but may stop early based on a quality confidence interval. BARGAIN (Zeighami et al., 2025) considers metrics such as accuracy and recall, and proposes finer-grained estimation methods. These methods differ fundamentally from our setting, as they select a single model for an isolated task. In contrast, we select a specific LLM for each module within a compound AI system that handles multi-step tasks.

Using multiple models at runtime. Another line of work utilizes multiple LLMs via online routing or cascades, where queries are adaptively forwarded to different models during execution. FrugalGPT (Chen et al., 2024) invokes models sequentially from cheapest to most expensive, stopping once a learned confidence criterion is met. LLM-Cascade (Yue et al., 2024) combines lightweight models with a decision mechanism and a stronger fallback model. ThriftLLM (Huang et al., 2025a) selects a subset of LLMs to maximize quality under a cost constraint by aggregating their outputs at runtime. Similarly, the work by Atalar (2026) studies model selection along a pipeline with partial feedback using bandit-style algorithms. For a comprehensive survey of using multiple LLMs during execution, we refer readers to Chen et al. (2025b). However, these approaches target specific system architectures to enable query-dependent or dynamic routing. In contrast, our work focuses on configuring arbitrary compound AI systems. Furthermore, their objectives differ from ours: we minimize cost subject to a strict quality constraint.

6. Experiments

In this section, we evaluate SCOPE on various tasks with different compound AI systems, addressing the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: How does SCOPE improve correctness, effectiveness, and cost-efficiency compared to baseline approaches?

  • •

    RQ2: Does the solution returned by SCOPE generalize in test-time deployments?

  • •

    RQ3: How sensitive is the performance of SCOPE to different kernel and reference configuration settings?

We also conduct ablation studies on key components of SCOPE and additional scalability evaluations. Results are presented in Appendix B.

6.1. Experimental Setup

Problem settings. We run experiments on three data management tasks: Text-to-SQL, data transformation, and data imputation. We use the compound AI systems in DIN-SQL (Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023), UniDM-DT, and UniDM-DI (Qian et al., 2024) for these tasks, respectively. For each task, we adopt the dataset 𝒬\mathcal{Q} used in the system’s original paper, and set the maximum budget Λmax\Lambda_{\max} to approximately match the monetary cost incurred when random search runs for 20 iterations, which is sufficient for most methods to converge to a stable solution. Details are listed in Table 2. In addition, we construct the candidate model set ℳ\mathcal{M} with 23 models covering a wide range of prices and capabilities, resulting in search spaces containing tens of thousands to millions of configurations. The full LLM list is provided in Appendix A. We set 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} to the configuration in which all modules use GPT-5.2, the most expensive model in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and set ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01. We compute each yg,ty_{g,t} using the standard evaluation metric of the task, i.e., execution accuracy for Text-to-SQL and accuracy for data transformation and data imputation. We compute each yc,ty_{c,t} as the actual incurred cost in USD. For any configuration 𝜽\bm{\theta} reported in our experiments, we estimate c⁡(𝜽)c(\bm{\theta}) and s⁡(𝜽)s(\bm{\theta}) offline by evaluating 𝜽\bm{\theta} on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} multiple times and taking the average; these evaluations are not counted toward the budget of any method.

Competitors and configurations. We evaluate SCOPE against seven competitors, divided into two categories as follows.

  • •

    Generic optimizations: random search (Random), cEI (Wang et al., 2025), CONFIG (Xu et al., 2023), and SafeOpt (Sui et al., 2015). For these methods, we follow the standard implementations from prior work (Xu et al., 2023).

  • •

    Compound-AI-specific approaches: LLAMBO (Liu et al., 2024), LLMSelector (Chen et al., 2025a), and Abacus (Russo et al., 2025). We make the necessary minimal adaptations to align with the setting in Problem 1; see Appendix A for details.

For SCOPE and generic approaches that require an SPD kernel kk, we follow prior work (Snoek et al., 2012) and use the Matérn 5/25/2 kernel:

k⁡(𝜽,𝜽′)=(1+5​d​(𝜽,𝜽′)+53​d​(𝜽,𝜽′)2)​e−5​d​(𝜽,𝜽′),\textstyle k(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})=\left(1+\sqrt{5}\,d(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})+\tfrac{5}{3}d(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})^{2}\right)e^{-\sqrt{5}d(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})},\vskip-8.53581pt

where d⁡(𝜽,𝜽′)=∑i=1N𝟏{θi≠θ′i}d(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bm{1}\{\theta_{i}\neq\theta^{\prime}_{i}\}} counts the number of modules on which 𝜽\bm{\theta} and 𝜽′\bm{\theta}^{\prime} choose different LLMs. To ensure a fair comparison, we use the same kernel across these methods, although kernel choices may affect empirical performance. For SCOPE, we set Rc=Rg=10−3R_{c}=R_{g}=10^{-3}, δ=10−4\delta=10^{-4}, α=1/3\alpha=1/3, and θbase\theta_{\rm base} to Gemini-2.5-flash-lite. We treat BcB_{c} and BgB_{g} as hyperparameters and tune them before the main loop (Line 1 of Algorithm 1), so that Line 1 of Algorithm 1 has at least one eligible configuration when executing for the first time.

Evaluation metrics. For each task and search budget Λ∈[0,Λmax]\Lambda\in[0,\Lambda_{\max}], we mainly report metrics for each algorithm’s returned configuration, denoted as 𝜽out,Λ\bm{\theta}_{\rm out,\Lambda}. To evaluate effectiveness and cost-efficiency, we report the best feasible cost achieved by each algorithm up to budget Λ\Lambda, defined as

cbf(Λ)=minΛ′≤Λ:s⁡(𝜽out,Λ′)≥s0c(𝜽out,Λ′).c_{\rm bf}(\Lambda)=\min_{\Lambda^{\prime}\leq\Lambda:~s(\bm{\theta}_{\rm out,\Lambda^{\prime}})\geq s_{0}}c(\bm{\theta}_{\rm out,\Lambda^{\prime}}).

Specifically, effectiveness is represented by how small the best feasible cost is at the maximum budget Λmax\Lambda_{\max}. Cost-efficiency means how fast the best feasible cost reduces as the budget increases. For SCOPE and its variants, cbf​(Λ)=SR⁡(τ)+c⁡(𝜽⋆)c_{\rm bf}(\Lambda)=\mathrm{SR}(\tau)+c(\bm{\theta}^{\star}) at the returned stopping time τ\tau corresponding to budget Λ\Lambda. For other methods, it similarly represents the best cost found up to budget Λ\Lambda, where infeasible configurations are ruled out. To assess correctness, i.e., whether s⁡(𝜽out)≥s0s({\bm{\theta}}_{\rm out})\geq s_{0}, we also report the average constraint violation metric (Xu et al., 2023) up to budget Λ\Lambda, defined as

V⁡(Λ)=1Λ​∫0Λmax⁡{s0−s⁡(𝜽out,u),0}s0​𝑑u,\textstyle V(\Lambda)=\frac{1}{\Lambda}\int_{0}^{\Lambda}\frac{\max\{s_{0}-s(\bm{\theta}_{{\rm out},u}),0\}}{s_{0}}du,

with V⁡(0)=0V(0)=0. V⁡(Λ)V(\Lambda) measures the extent to which the returned configuration violates the quality constraint, and V⁡(Λ)=0V(\Lambda)=0 means that correctness holds at all budgets from 00 to Λ\Lambda. Since there are finitely many different 𝜽out,u\bm{\theta}_{{\rm out},u}, we compute the integral exactly by summing over the corresponding budget intervals. We repeat each experiment three times, each with a fixed random seed, and report the median, minimum, and maximum values. All experiments were conducted on a Linux server equipped with an Intel Xeon(R) Gold 6240 CPU @ 2.60GHz and 377GB of RAM, using multi-threading to maximize throughput when invoking LLMs. The implementations of all algorithms are available at https://github.com/waetr/SCOPE-LLM-optimizer/.

6.2. Performance Evaluation (RQ1)

In the first set of experiments, we evaluate SCOPE against competitors in the three tasks, varying the search budget Λ∈[0,Λmax]\Lambda\in[0,\Lambda_{\max}]. Figure 1 reports the best feasible cost cbf​(Λ)c_{\rm bf}(\Lambda) and the constraint violation V⁡(Λ)V(\Lambda) of each algorithm. For better visualization, we report only the median of V⁡(Λ)V(\Lambda) for LLMSelector across the three runs, as its maximum (up to 0.640.64) would dominate most of the figure.

Effectiveness and efficiency. As shown in the upper panels of Figure 1, SCOPE consistently outperforms all competitors in terms of the final best feasible cost and how fast the cost converges. Specifically, at the maximum budget Λmax\Lambda_{\max}, cbf​(Λmax)c_{\rm bf}(\Lambda_{\max}) found by SCOPE is 83.7%83.7\%, 53.5%53.5\%, and 21.1%21.1\% lower than that of the best competitor in Text-to-SQL, data transformation, and data imputation, respectively. Furthermore, across budgets Λ∈[0,Λmax]\Lambda\in[0,\Lambda_{\max}], SCOPE achieves up to 95.5%95.5\%, 63.1%63.1\%, and 93.6%93.6\% lower best feasible cost cbf​(Λ)c_{\rm bf}(\Lambda) than the best competitor in the three tasks, respectively. The lower best feasible cost at Λmax\Lambda_{\max} suggests that the candidates 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} selected by SCOPE have strong cost and quality under the confidence-bound-based selection criterion. During search, the rapid improvement in cbf​(Λ)c_{\rm bf}(\Lambda) is driven by SCOPE’s exploitation of query-level observations: compared with competitors that rely on dataset-level evaluation and thus must spend a full pass over 𝒬\mathcal{Q} for each configuration, SCOPE can rule out many infeasible or suboptimal candidates after evaluating only a few queries (e.g., in data imputation, we observe that 79% of 𝜽cand\bm{\theta}_{\rm cand} considered by SCOPE are ruled out after evaluating the first 40 queries), saving substantial search budget. In addition, the Calibrate subroutine evaluates many good configurations at a small budget, unlike other competitors that often fail to obtain a good starting point during search. Regarding other competitors, the performance among cEI, CONFIG, LLAMBO, and Abacus varies substantially across different tasks, in contrast to the consistently strong performance of SCOPE. LLMSelector rarely finds a better solution than 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} across the three tasks, as it overemphasizes quality while overlooking cost. SafeOpt also performs conservatively, as it enforces that every evaluated configuration must be feasible, which limits exploration of potentially better ones. To summarize, SCOPE is significantly more cost-efficient and effective than all competitors.

Correctness. As shown in the lower panels of Figure 1, SCOPE exhibits zero constraint violations V⁡(Λ)V(\Lambda) across all tasks and budgets, aligning with its δ\delta-correctness guarantee in theory. Regarding other methods, SafeOpt also has zero violations and, in theory, ensures correctness under the same assumptions as SCOPE. cEI offers correctness only under a noiseless assumption; nonetheless, it also has zero violations in our experiments. The remaining methods exhibit oscillating or increasing V⁡(Λ)V(\Lambda), often due to the inductive biases of their estimation models, for which correctness guarantees are unknown.

6.3. Deployment Performance (RQ2)

In the second set of experiments, we evaluate, on a test-time dataset distinct from 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, the reported configuration at budget Λmax\Lambda_{\rm max} in Figure 1 (i.e., the one achieving the best feasible cost on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} within budget Λmax\Lambda_{\rm max}). The test-time datasets are listed in Table 2 and have been used as held-out test sets corresponding to 𝒬\mathcal{Q} (Qian et al., 2024). Table 3 reports the resulting average cost and average quality on these datasets. Overall, the average costs at test time are within the same order of magnitude as those on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. In addition, some methods achieve cost reductions while maintaining average quality comparable to the reference configuration 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}, demonstrating the presence of configurations with lower cost than the expensive single-model baseline without sacrificing potential quality.

Performance of SCOPE. Notably, the configuration found by SCOPE on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} generalizes well: SCOPE attains the lowest average cost among all methods while achieving higher average quality than the reference configuration 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}. Concretely, in Text-to-SQL, data transformation, and data imputation, the average costs of SCOPE are only 3%3\%, 5%5\%, and 2%2\% of those of 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}, respectively. Furthermore, its average quality improves upon 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} by 21%21\%, 5%5\%, and 19%19\%. We attribute this surprising quality improvement to the way SCOPE ensures δ\delta-correctness under noisy evaluations. As feasibility must be certified with high probability, SCOPE is less likely to return configurations that sit right near the quality threshold on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Instead, it tends to select configurations with a meaningful quality margin (i.e., the part exceeding the quality threshold). Under dataset shift, this margin makes the selected configuration more likely to remain feasible and, in some cases, even to outperform 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} in average quality.

Performance of other competitors. In contrast to SCOPE, other competitors translate less reliably to test time. They achieve much smaller cost savings and may fail to match the average quality of 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}. For example, cEI’s average costs are 13.1×13.1\times, 13.8×13.8\times, and 10.2×10.2\times larger than those of SCOPE across the three tasks. In data transformation, its average quality is 8%8\% lower than that of 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}. This reflects the brittleness of its correctness property under a noiseless assumption: by choosing solutions very close to the quality threshold, cEI can overfit to 𝒬\mathcal{Q} rather than yield robust test-time performance. Similarly, CONFIG and LLAMBO exhibit lower average quality than 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} in data transformation, as they lack mechanisms to generalize beyond 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Meanwhile, while SafeOpt maintains feasibility on these datasets, it realizes cost reductions much smaller than SCOPE, similar to its behavior during search. The remaining methods, Abacus and LLMSelector, achieve average quality no worse than that of 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}, but still incur average costs at least 6×6\times higher than SCOPE. In sum, SCOPE reduces more cost than other competitors, while delivering improved quality relative to the reference configuration on held-out queries.

6.4. Sensitivity Analysis (RQ3)

In the third set of experiments, we evaluate whether SCOPE’s performance is sensitive to two settings used in the main experiments: the reference configuration 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} in the problem definition and the kernel k⁡(⋅,⋅)k(\cdot,\cdot) in SCOPE. We use data imputation for illustration and keep the other experiment settings the same as in Section 6.2. We compare the best feasible cost of SCOPE with that of the strongest competitors, cEI and CONFIG, over the search budget Λ\Lambda.

Reference configuration. We first replace the default reference configuration with one in which all modules use Claude Haiku 4.5. As shown in Figure 2(a), SCOPE remains effective under this change and attains the lowest best feasible cost once the budget exceeds 1.21.2 USD. This shows that the improvement of SCOPE is not tied to a specific reference configuration.

Kernel. We next replace the Matérn 5/25/2 kernel with the squared exponential (SE) kernel, defined as k(𝜽,𝜽′)=exp(−d(𝜽,𝜽′)2/2).k(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})=\exp(-d(\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime})^{2}/2). As shown in Figure 2(b), SCOPE continues to achieve lower best feasible cost than the other kernel-based competitors without intensive kernel tuning. Specifically, at Λmax\Lambda_{\rm max}, the best feasible cost of SCOPE is at most 50%50\% of that of the second-best method. As a practical guideline, one can start with the default Matérn 5/25/2 kernel and use the SE kernel only if needed.

7. Conclusion

We study constrained LLM selection for compound AI systems. To solve this problem, we propose SCOPE, a search algorithm that exploits query-level partial evaluations and provides high-probability feasibility and simple-regret guarantees. In experiments, SCOPE reduces search cost relative to state-of-the-art baselines while better satisfying the quality constraint across multiple tasks. For future work, we plan to extend SCOPE to richer representations of cost–quality trade-offs, including multi-objective optimization and multiple constraints.

Appendix A Experiment Details

Candidate LLMs. The candidate LLMs used in the experiments are listed in Table 4. The pricing values are obtained from the official OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and DeepInfra platforms as of the submission date. According to these platforms, the cost incurred by invoking an LLM equals (# input tokens) ×\times (input price) ++ (# output tokens) ×\times (output price).

Adaptation details. LLAMBO uses natural language instructions to prompt an LLM to emulate the BO process, where each instruction includes metadata about the compound AI system, the dataset, the candidate LLMs, and the past observation history. We adapt the instruction template from the original paper (Liu et al., 2024) to extend it to the constrained setting. The underlying LLM for estimation is GPT-5.2. LLMSelector (Chen et al., 2025a) maximizes the quality ss by sequentially updating the LLM configuration starting from a random configuration, without considering cost. In addition, it optionally adopts an LLM diagnostician to analyze the intermediate quality of each module to guide the search. We remove this diagnostician since such intermediate quality is unavailable. Abacus conducts a bandit-style sequential search on sampled query subsets of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, but its core mechanism requires knowing the model-wise quality of each module. To obtain this, in each iteration, we evaluate two configurations, where one is obtained from the other by changing the model choice in the module the algorithm is currently searching over. For random search, we iteratively evaluate a configuration randomly sampled from Θ\Theta without replacement on the entire dataset 𝒬\mathcal{Q} until the search budget is exhausted.

Appendix B Ablation and Scalability Studies

In this section, we conduct ablation studies on key components and parameter settings of SCOPE and scalability evaluations on larger datasets.

Ablation study. We compare SCOPE with two variants, SCOPE-Rand and SCOPE-Coarse. SCOPE-Rand replaces Θinit\Theta_{\rm init} in Line 2 of the Calibrate subroutine (Algorithm 2) with a set of configurations sampled uniformly at random from Θ\Theta, with the same size as Θinit\Theta_{\rm init}. SCOPE-Coarse removes Calibrate and Line 1 from Algorithm 1, and sets t0=0t_{0}=0. As a result, neither SCOPE-Rand nor SCOPE-Coarse requires θbase\theta_{\rm base} as input, and SCOPE-Coarse evaluates the entire dataset in every iteration ii until the budget is exhausted.

Figure 3 reports the best feasible cost cbf​(Λ)c_{\rm bf}(\Lambda) versus the search budget Λ\Lambda. We also conduct experiments varying other input parameters; across budgets and tasks, all three methods exhibit zero violations, and the output of SCOPE remains unchanged for α∈[1/5,1/2−10−9]\alpha\in[1/5,1/2-10^{-9}] and δ∈[10−5,10−3]\delta\in[10^{-5},10^{-3}]. As shown by SCOPE-Rand, replacing Θinit\Theta_{\rm init} in (3) with a random configuration makes SCOPE-Rand improve upon 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} more slowly than SCOPE at small budgets. For example, in Text-to-SQL, SCOPE reduces cbfc_{\rm bf} to 2.6×10−32.6\times 10^{-3} by Λ=5.5\Lambda=5.5, whereas SCOPE-Rand first improves upon 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} only at Λ=11.0\Lambda=11.0. This is because the randomly sampled configurations can be more expensive, leading to a higher initialization cost and delaying subsequent search progress in terms of budget. However, after surpassing 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}, SCOPE-Rand often converges faster than SCOPE. For instance, in data imputation, SCOPE-Rand reduces the cost to 5.5×10−55.5\times 10^{-5} before Λ=0.9\Lambda=0.9, even lower than SCOPE’s best feasible cost at Λmax\Lambda_{\rm max}. To explain, a random configuration set can cover Θ\Theta more broadly, which may improve Calibrate over diverse configurations and help identify better candidates, although this advantage is unstable due to sampling randomness. In contrast, SCOPE-Coarse converges much more slowly than SCOPE. For instance, at Λmax\Lambda_{\rm max}, its best feasible cost is about 3−5×3-5\times higher than that of SCOPE, yet still lower than that of cEI, across tasks. While the guarantees in Theorem 4.2 can also apply to SCOPE-Coarse if Q=1Q=1, SCOPE-Coarse discards query-level signal exploitation and thus falls back to dataset-level evaluations, inheriting the cost inefficiency of existing competitors.

Scalability evaluation. To further validate SCOPE’s performance, we experiment on an additional task, entity resolution, with a 3-module UniDM-ER system and dataset Amazon-google-dev of 2293 queries (Qian et al., 2024). Figure 4 shows the best feasible cost of each method over the search budget. At the maximum budget, SCOPE is superior to other competitors in this new task, similar to the trends reflected in the original experiments. Specifically, the best feasible cost of SCOPE is 97% lower than that of the reference configuration, and 50% lower than that of the second-best method, LLAMBO.

Algorithm. Recall that at time tt, the observation history in an algorithm is Ht={(𝜽i,qi,yc,i,yg,i)}i=1tH_{t}=\{(\bm{\theta}_{i},q_{i},y_{c,i},y_{g,i})\}_{i=1}^{t}, with H0=∅H_{0}=\emptyset.   • •

    τ\tau is a stopping time with respect to the filtration (ℱt)t=0∞(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{\infty};

    (πt)t=1∞(\pi_{t})_{t=1}^{\infty} is a sequence of ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable mappings. For each t≥1t\geq 1, πt\pi_{t} maps Ht−1H_{t-1} to a probability distribution over Θ×𝒬\Theta\times\mathcal{Q}, denoted by πt(⋅|Ht−1)\pi_{t}(\cdot|H_{t-1}). At each time tt (for 1≤t≤τ1\leq t\leq\tau), the pair (𝜽t,qt)(\bm{\theta}_{t},q_{t}) is sampled from πt(⋅|Ht−1)\pi_{t}(\cdot|H_{t-1}), yielding observations yc,ty_{c,t} and yg,ty_{g,t};

    𝜽out∈Θ\bm{\theta}_{\rm{out}}\in\Theta is an ℱτ\mathcal{F}_{\tau}-measurable random variable representing the algorithm’s recommendation of the best configuration.

C.2. Proof of Theorem 4.1

We first establish a query-wise confidence bound for each GP (one per query qq and metric ζ\zeta), and then aggregate across queries to obtain a confidence bound for the dataset-average metric. Recall Jq,t=|𝒥q,t|J_{q,t}=|\mathcal{J}_{q,t}| and let jq​(1)<⋯<jq​(J)j_{q}(1)<\cdots<j_{q}(J) be the times when query qq is evaluated up to time tt. For fixed (q,ζ,t)(q,\zeta,t), define 𝜽(a)=𝜽jq​(a)\bm{\theta}^{(a)}=\bm{\theta}_{j_{q}(a)} and y(a)=yζ,jq​(a)y^{(a)}=y_{\zeta,j_{q}(a)} for a∈[J]a\in[J], and let J=Jq,tJ=J_{q,t}.

We use the following standard kernelized self-normalized inequality (see, e.g., Theorem 1 and Lemma 1 of (Chowdhury and Gopalan, 2017)).

Lemma C.1 (Kernelized self-normalization).

Let (𝛉(a),η(a))a≥1(\bm{\theta}^{(a)},\eta^{(a)})_{a\geq 1} be a (possibly adaptive) sequence such that η(a)\eta^{(a)} is conditionally RR-sub-Gaussian w.r.t. the filtration generated by the past. Then for any δ′∈(0,1)\delta^{\prime}\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ′1-\delta^{\prime}, simultaneously for all J≥1J\geq 1,

‖SJ‖VJ−1≤R​2​(ℐJ+log⁡1δ′)≤R​2​(γ​(J)+log⁡1δ′),\|S_{J}\|_{V_{J}^{-1}}\leq R\sqrt{2\Big(\mathcal{I}_{J}+\log\frac{1}{\delta^{\prime}}\Big)}\leq R\sqrt{2\Big(\gamma(J)+\log\frac{1}{\delta^{\prime}}\Big)},

Proof outline for simple regret. We focus on rounds where the selection threshold is small enough that 𝜽⋆\bm{\theta}^{\star} satisfies the constraint in Line 1. For these rounds, the selection rule guarantees that the chosen candidate has a cost lower confidence bound no larger than that of 𝜽⋆\bm{\theta}^{\star}, so SR\mathrm{SR} can be controlled by the cost confidence width. We then bound SR\mathrm{SR} by the smallest such width among candidates that are eventually certified feasible, and replace this minimum by an average over the certified-feasible rounds, which introduces an inverse dependence on their count. Finally, we lower bound the number of certified-feasible rounds: any round that is not certified feasible must exhibit sufficiently large constraint uncertainty relative to its threshold, while the total accumulated constraint uncertainty is bounded. Combining the two steps yields the stated SR\mathrm{SR} bound.

Appendix D Tightness Results

To show that the dependence Ω⁡(1/(Δ⋆)2)\Omega(1/(\Delta^{\star})^{2}) cannot be removed from any convergent simple-regret guarantee under Problem 1, where Δ⋆=−g⁡(𝜽⋆)\Delta^{\star}=-g(\bm{\theta}^{\star}), we construct a set of counterexamples. Let Q=1Q=1, 𝒬={q}\mathcal{Q}=\{q\}, Θ={𝜽0,𝜽1}\Theta=\{\bm{\theta}_{0},\bm{\theta}_{1}\}, s⁡(𝜽0)=1s(\bm{\theta}_{0})=1, ϵ=1/2\epsilon=1/2, c⁡(𝜽0)=1c(\bm{\theta}_{0})=1 and c⁡(𝜽1)=0c(\bm{\theta}_{1})=0, so s0=1/2s_{0}=1/2. For each Δ∈(0,1/2]\Delta\in(0,1/2], define two instances

ℐΔ+:s⁡(𝜽1)=1/2+Δ,ℐΔ−:s⁡(𝜽1)=1/2−Δ.\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\Delta}:s(\bm{\theta}_{1})=1/2+\Delta,\quad\mathcal{I}^{-}_{\Delta}:s(\bm{\theta}_{1})=1/2-\Delta.

Assume that the observations on gg satisfy yg,t=g⁡(𝜽t)+ηty_{g,t}=g(\bm{\theta}_{t})+\eta_{t} with ηt∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\eta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), and the observations on cc satisfy yc,t=c⁡(𝜽t)y_{c,t}=c(\bm{\theta}_{t}). One can verify that these instances satisfy Assumptions 1–2 with fixed constants.

Fix δ∈(0,1/4)\delta\in(0,1/4) and an integer τ∈ℕ\tau\in\mathbb{N}. Let π\pi be any adaptive algorithm that makes τ\tau observations and outputs 𝜽out∈Θ\bm{\theta}_{\rm out}\in\Theta. Assume that for every Δ∈(0,1/2]\Delta\in(0,1/2], when the true instance is ℐΔ−\mathcal{I}^{-}_{\Delta}, the algorithm is δ\delta-correct. The impossibility theorem follows.

Theorem D.1.

Under the above construction, on ℐΔ+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\Delta} the simple regret satisfies

(35) 𝔼⁡[SR⁡(τ)]≥(1−δ−Δ⋆​τ)+,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{SR}(\tau)\right]\ \geq\ \left(1-\delta-\Delta^{\star}\sqrt{\tau}\right)_{+},

and in particular, any guarantee of the form 𝔼⁡[SR⁡(τ)]≤ε\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SR}(\tau)]\leq\varepsilon with ε<1−δ\varepsilon<1-\delta requires

τ≥(1−δ−ε)2(Δ⋆)2=Ω⁡(1(Δ⋆)2).\tau\ \geq\ \frac{(1-\delta-\varepsilon)^{2}}{(\Delta^{\star})^{2}}\ =\ \Omega\!\left(\frac{1}{(\Delta^{\star})^{2}}\right).
Proof.

Fix Δ∈(0,1/2]\Delta\in(0,1/2] and define the event A={𝜽out=𝜽1}A=\{\bm{\theta}_{\rm out}=\bm{\theta}_{1}\}. On ℐΔ−\mathcal{I}^{-}_{\Delta}, 𝜽1\bm{\theta}_{1} is infeasible since g⁡(𝜽1)=Δ>0g(\bm{\theta}_{1})=\Delta>0. Therefore, δ\delta-correctness implies PrℐΔ−⁡(A)≤δ\Pr_{\mathcal{I}^{-}_{\Delta}}(A)\leq\delta.

Let P−ΔP_{-\Delta} and P+ΔP_{+\Delta} denote the joint laws of the full transcript under ℐΔ−\mathcal{I}^{-}_{\Delta} and ℐΔ+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\Delta}. Let N1=∑t=1τ𝟏{𝜽t=𝜽1}N_{1}=\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\bm{1}\{\bm{\theta}_{t}=\bm{\theta}_{1}\} be the number of evaluations of 𝜽1\bm{\theta}_{1}, so N1≤τN_{1}\leq\tau almost surely. The two instances differ only in the distribution of yg,ty_{g,t} when 𝜽t=𝜽1\bm{\theta}_{t}=\bm{\theta}_{1}. Under ℐΔ−\mathcal{I}^{-}_{\Delta}, yg,t∼𝒩⁡(Δ,1)y_{g,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\Delta,1), while under ℐΔ+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\Delta}, yg,t∼𝒩⁡(−Δ,1)y_{g,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(-\Delta,1). Using the chain rule for KL divergence under adaptive sampling (Kaufmann et al., 2016), we have

KL(P−Δ∥P+Δ)\displaystyle{\rm KL}(P_{-\Delta}\,\|\,P_{+\Delta}) =𝔼−Δ[N1]⋅KL(𝒩(Δ,1)∥𝒩(−Δ,1))\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{-\Delta}[N_{1}]\cdot{\rm KL}(\mathcal{N}(\Delta,1)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(-\Delta,1))
=𝔼−Δ​[N1]⋅2​Δ2≤ 2​τ​Δ2.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{-\Delta}[N_{1}]\cdot 2\Delta^{2}\ \leq\ 2\tau\Delta^{2}.

‖P−Δ−P+Δ‖TV≤KL(P−Δ∥P+Δ)/2≤Δ​τ.\|P_{-\Delta}-P_{+\Delta}\|_{\rm TV}\ \leq\ \sqrt{{\rm KL}(P_{-\Delta}\,\|\,P_{+\Delta})/2}\ \leq\ \Delta\sqrt{\tau}.

Therefore

PrℐΔ+⁡(A)≤PrℐΔ−⁡(A)+‖P−Δ−P+Δ‖TV≤δ+Δ​τ,\Pr_{\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\Delta}}(A)\leq\Pr_{\mathcal{I}^{-}_{\Delta}}(A)+\|P_{-\Delta}-P_{+\Delta}\|_{\rm TV}\leq\delta+\Delta\sqrt{\tau},

and hence PrℐΔ+⁡(Ac)≥(1−δ−Δ​τ)+\Pr_{\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\Delta}}(A^{c})\geq(1-\delta-\Delta\sqrt{\tau})_{+}.

On ℐΔ+\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\Delta}, 𝜽1\bm{\theta}_{1} is feasible and optimal since c⁡(𝜽1)=0<c⁡(𝜽0)=1c(\bm{\theta}_{1})=0<c(\bm{\theta}_{0})=1, so 𝜽⋆=𝜽1\bm{\theta}^{\star}=\bm{\theta}_{1} and Δ⋆=−g⁡(𝜽⋆)=Δ\Delta^{\star}=-g(\bm{\theta}^{\star})=\Delta. Thus SR⁡(τ)=1\mathrm{SR}(\tau)=1 exactly on AcA^{c}, and 𝔼⁡[SR⁡(τ)]=Pr⁡(Ac)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SR}(\tau)]=\Pr(A^{c}). Substituting Δ⋆=Δ\Delta^{\star}=\Delta yields (35).
